That Bill C-136 be amended by adding immediately after line 6 at page 57 the following:
"92.(1) Five years after the coming into force of this Act a comprehensive review of the provisions and operation of Sections 7, 8, 19, 26 and 27 of this Act, including the effect of such provisions, shall be undertaken by such committee of the House of Commons as may be designated or established by the House for that purpose.
(2) Within six months after the completion of the review referred to in subsection (1), the committee so designated or established for that purpose shall submit a report on the review to Parliament including a statement of any changes to the committee would recommend."

September 23, 1988
Broadcasting Act
She said: I am pleased to rise to discuss Motion No. 79 which is a sunset clause. It is a clause that would provide for an automatic review in five years after the coming into force of this Act. It is an identical review clause that the Minister included in her employment equity Bill, Bill C-62, when she was Minister of Employment and Immigration. I would like to suggest to the Minister that we are setting no precedents here. We are being consistent in asking for consideration of the implications of this Bill which has been seen as quite flawed by many of the players in this particular broadcast area.
This review clause has some specific provisions which would provide for the comprehensive review of the operations of Clauses 7 and 8, which are the CRTC clauses. Under the CRTC we have an established panel. That panel system has had a series of different points of view. Some call it the "Meechifying" of Canada. Some have referred to it as a serious mechanism that can, in a sense, destroy the national broadcasting system in terms of providing the kind of broadcast policy that would be evenly applied across this country. If we do not have a built-in review system we will not know just how this is working. Will regional commissioners be captured by their regional responsibility and become advocates for their region instead of proponents of a policy for a national broadcasting system?
The second area of concern I have highlighted is with respect to Clause 19 which, as I said, provides the CRTC panels. Clauses 7 and 8 are the Governor in Council power of direction. The Minister feels she has removed the potential for arm's length incursions in this Bill. It is true she has removed a number of them but there is still, in my view, one that remains which could create some very serious interventions, not just arm's length interventions but shoulder to wrist intervention by the Minister. Clauses 26 and 27, with respect to the Governor in Council variance and review of the CRTC decisions, fall into the same bloc.
There were a lot of concerns and because the debate was split, I think with this motion we would be rendering the best of service. Although I have not clearly enunciated other provisions, I would suggest that we are going to have to look at this because the Minister has not accepted further definition or clarity as to what has happened at the CBC in light of the fact that there is no real boss defined. Has this Bill "Meechified" Canada's Broadcasting Act, as was suggested by Mr. William Johnson? Are we having the separate standing committees that are in the CBC now as a mandate rather than as a decision of the board, which would be the normal structure? How is that going to affect the radio and television sense of delivery of service to Anglophone minorities in Quebec in areas like Chicoutimi, Gaspe, the Outaouais, and Sherbrooke, the small towns across this country, not to mention the large cities such as Montreal? What is going to happen to the Francophones in Saskatoon, Regina, Manitoba and Winnipeg? Will the services be delivered in an equitable way if we have divided this board of directors the way the Minister directs in this Bill?
What will be the impact of the lack of clarity of the definition of broadcasting, the fact that the deregulation of the programming services into non-programming services which will not fall under the CRTC telecom side rather than the broadcast side? What will happen with respect to fair and due process and the fact that we have given the CRTC a mandate that allows it to develop the rules, examine them, apply them and fine people when these rules are not being applied, in other words, be judge and jury in its own case? It is really a very unfair principle in law and we are concerned about that.
What about the bottom line, the free trade agreement? Has it really affected our radio song content? Has it allowed for the Americanization of our network because we have not decided we would control the number of American stations that can come in? We have not decided to license. We have not accepted the grandfathering of the 22 American stations that come in on our TV sets. It is of ongoing concern that this supposed Canadian broadcasting policy will enable the Canadian people to have the option of good Canadian programming when they select their Canadian channels.
As we well know, we have a situation where we have a hybrid cable system which we are allowing to expand, and we do not know the impact of it, we have an American system mixed with ours, and our own system carries those American networks, and we are now demanding more and more from our broadcasting in terms of input of money and production of good quality programs. These are all valued goals, but will they be met under this Broadcasting Act? There is a big question mark at this time.
I have requested serious consideration by the Minister of a sunset clause which will be consistent with other clauses that have been undertaken by Governments. I would just add one other point. We have been very concerned about the CBC and five-year funding. Whereas we demand a five-year operational plan, which is good business sense, we are not prepared to give CBC the dollars to put it into effect.
All in all, I would like to recommend strongly the acceptance of Motion No. 79 which would add a new Clause 92.1 at the end of the broadcasting Bill, Bill C-136, to ensure that the experience and examples which I have just outlined have been properly effective in order to have a strong Canadian broadcasting system from coast to coast for English and French constituents, whether their mother tongue is English or French or whether they are watching because they wish to appreciate another culture, learn another language or just see themselves expressed in that particular perspective.

Mr. Speaker, this group we are debating now is our final group of amendments. It only includes Motion No. 79 from the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone). It is a sunset clause for all the provisions which change the Government's power vis-a-vis the CRTC, the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission, which is the over-all regulator of broadcasting in Canada, and the change in the decisionmaking practices of the CRTC itself. It states that after five years a committee of Parliament shall review the effects of those changes, and so on.
September 23, 1988

As I mentioned earlier this week, on the specific matter of the CRTC, the Minister and I, with a few exceptions, are more or less on the same wave length. This was not always the case. I think we in the legislative committee can take some credit for having improved this aspect of the Bill in the short and rushed time in which we dealt with the Bill in committee.
The Minister's original plans for the CRTC were objected to by almost all the witnesses who appeared before the committee. There were significant concerns expressed about whether the decentralization of the CRTC would have a profound affect on the consistency of the commission and whether the powers taken by the Governor in Council, the Cabinet, if you like, Mr. Speaker, would lead to excessive political interference in the affairs of the commission.
Fortunately, at the legislative committee, and to the credit of the Minister, we were able to pass five important amendments which improved this part of the Bill. I am pleased to say we were able to propose many of these amendments. The first amendment was to Clause 7 of the Bill. This ensured that if the Government used its power of policy direction, the directions themselves would be broad and of general application, not specific. These amendments brought substantially greater clarity to the Act and I think reflected in effect the original intent of the Minister, in any event.
The second amendment was to Clause 19 and ensures that the new panels that will be established to make CRTC decisions-the principle is that she or he who hears decides- shall consist of at least two full-time members in order to ensure consistency. I believe Ray Peters of BCTV, among other people, made this suggestion. I moved the amendment and it was incorporated in Clause 19.
The third amendment also applies to Clause 19 and suggests that members of the panel shall consult with other members of the commission in making their decisions.
The fourth amendment was the deletion of Clause 26 in the original Bill which was the Government's power of exemption. This was deemed by just about everyone to be an excessive and potentially dangerous power.
The final amendment extended the term of part-time commissioners from three to five years. As was mentioned by someone in the committee, three years on the CRTC apparently barely gives commissioners time to find the washroom.
The amendment proposed in Clause 79 by my hon. friend from Mount Royal is a positive one 1 think. Our legislative committee sat for a short time and yet we made some fundamental corrections to clauses in this Bill. I think most Canadians would agree with the statement that Members of Parliament, no more or less than the Minister of Communications, are not infallible.
These clauses represent an important change to the structure of regulatory affairs in this country. 1 think that after five years we should have a pretty good sense of how they are
Broadcasting Act
working in practice. 1 therefore support the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member in order to ensure that a review is conducted to see how we are doing after that period.
That is the end of my remarks on that particular amendment. I am pleased that the ministry accepted some amendments. 1 think that is the way we should do things in Parliament. I hope that before the Bill is finally voted on the Minister will have a look at some of the other amendments that were rejected, perhaps in the heat of the debate here in the House. Perhaps with altered wording or some adjustments the Minister might accept them. I think of Clause 39 and Clause 35 and others in that area which dealt with Canadiani-zation of the air waves which tried to reflect, we thought, the recommendations of the all-Party committee on broadcasting.

Mr. Speaker, in support of Motion No. 79 moved by the Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), I would like to put on record the concerns expressed by the Canadian Bar Association whose brief, it is my understanding, was not studied in committee. That is regrettable because the brief by the Canadian Bar Association contains a number of very interesting and significant observations which ought to be taken into account.
I will give you three examples. One, the Canadian Bar Association expresses the desirability and concern that this Bill ought to be consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Without going into details, obviously the Canadian Bar Association would not express such a preoccupation if it had not concluded that this Bill needs to be brought in line and made consistent with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
This is, of course, very important legislation and the Bar Association says that very little time was given to interested groups to review the draft language of Bill C-136. It is in this context that the submission and input from the Canadian Bar Association is to be seen. For the life of me I cannot understand why a Bill of this significance was moved through the committee with such speed.
Second, the Canadian Bar Association expresses the view that the Act should be sensitive to questions of fairness and due process in the administrative law context. One need not elaborate on that. That is an observation of substance which says it all.
The Canadian Bar Association makes the most important point in its submission when it addresses another aspect of Bill C-136. It urges that the language should be clear, unambiguous, and readily understandable. We all know that it often happens that legislation is drafted in an obscure manner. This observation applies to Bill C-136 as well as to other pieces of legislation that we tend to look upon in a rather technical manner and not from the review point of the layperson who wants to understand the substance and the message in that particular legislation.

September 23, 1988
Broadcasting Act
It is also important to put on record the views expressed by some observers in the fourth estate. I was rather struck by an article by William Johnson in The Gazette. He made the observation that this Bill "threatens the unity of Canada as a community of communications. It contains within it the seeds of fragmentation." That is part of the Meech Lake virus that is now permeating and penetrating a number of executive measures as well as legislation such as this in particular.
It is interesting to note how The Gazette, through Mr. Johnson, goes on in analysing this Bill. It says:
The bill attempts to decentralize the decision-making of the one body in this country which ensures the integrity, the consistency, the adequacy, the national purpose of our far-flung system of radio and television: the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC).
It abolishes the executive committee of the CRTC, which till now made most of the day-to-day decisions.
The new regional commissioners, resident in their region, backed by a regionally hired staff, will be considered as spokesmen and champions of that region. They will lose touch with the coherent, country-wide vision of broadcasting which now animates the collegial decision-making of the CRTC members who sit together in the capital.
As the media and communications loss actions of the Canadian Bar Association argued in their submission to the parliamentary committee, the "he who hears decides" principle is chiefly important where facts, not policies, are the relevent consideration of the hearings. That is a very important basic consideration.
The article continues:
To meet some of the criticisms, the government made changes to the bill requiring that at least two, and not just one, of the members of a panel must be full-time CRTC members, and further requiring that the panel members, before a decision, "shall consult other members of the commission or any officer of the commission for the purpose of ensuring a consistency of interpretation of the broadcasting policy.
But fragmentation remains likely when just two members of the CRTC can make fundamental decisions for the whole CRTC.
You can see that this analysis is very distressing because it shows that we are dismantling national unity. We are decentralizing, evidently. Therefore, we are heading for a system of broadcasting which will probably make the network system an assembly of original systems at the expense of a national system as we have known it so far.
I wonder whether the Minister is not distressed, knowing her stand in previous decades about what Canada is all about, by the trend she is now allowing to be set in motion through this Bill. I wonder whether she is comfortable with this notion of regionalizing the Canadian radio and television system the way this Bill is now attempting to do.
It is important that this amendment by the Member for Mount Royal not only be aired and put on record, because it would provide a sunset clause for an automatic review five years after the coming into force of the legislation, but that it give an opportunity for interested Members to express their views and support it in the hope that at least we will have this experiment of regionalism limited to five years rather than become a permanent feature in our radio and television system.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment very briefly on Motion No. 79 in the name of the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), a motion I believe will ensure that Canadians can expect a review of the performance of the CRTC every five years. [English]
Motion No. 79 is very good. It is what is called in legislative language a sunset clause motion. In other words, it includes in the Bill a review process automatically after five years of the coming into force of the Act. The provisions of this clause allow for a comprehensive review of Clauses 7 and 9 that provide for the Governor in Council to give direction to the CRTC. I want to address this subject because it touches on a very difficult and sometimes very sensitive point.
[ Translation]
Recently, Mr. Speaker, I read a CRTC press release, which contains some interesting statements. According to the CRTC, we have one of the best systems in the world, and I would like to quote verbatim from the press release dated September 14, 1988. This was fairly recent, when they published their annual report. I quote:
We know how highly regarded Canada's broadcasting system is, by the number of delegations from abroad who visit the CRTC to examine our system. These outside observers are awestruck by our achievements and continuing progress. .. They want to know how we have handled the overwhelming American presence over the years. Until now, Europeans, Australians, and others have been isolated from the impact of American broadcasting. But the reality of satellite communications has forced them to face this problem, and they look to the Canadian experience for guidance.
Mr. Speaker, that is what I mean when I ask the Government to give Canadians access to programming and to ensure that cable TV distributors transmit the TV5 signal. That is the point I am trying to make. I want French-speaking Canadians living outside Quebec, and I am one of them, to have access to TV5, and I want the CRTC, supported by the Government, to ensure the signal is available. All week people have been saying: Gauthier, don't be so impatient! This week the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said to the media: It is an excellent system. I agree. But we don't have it, and even when we do, it is incomplete.
For instance in Ottawa, the capital of this country only half the city gets TV5 and Canal Famille, and only those two, instead of the five signals they get in Quebec. We pay six dollars. East of the Rideau Canal, we pay six dollars more to have access to this program, while in Quebec it only costs $1.63 for all five signals. I think that is unfair. I think the Government should do something. I want to ask the Government and the CRTC to take the necessary action so that we can honestly say: Yes, we do have Canadian programming and we have taken steps to ensure this programming is diversified and meets the needs of our various communities. That is all 1 ask. I am not impatient. I just wonder why Ottawa Cablevision west of Bronson, in Ottawa, the capital of this country, says; No, we don't provide the TV5 signal. We are an English station, an English company. That is the answer we got this week. I don't understand that.
September 23, 1988

There are Francophones living in the western part of Ottawa, and there are Francophones living across this country, but cable TV does not give them acess to adequate programming. And as the CRTC's annual report says, we have managed to counter American influence and Amrican programming, and God knows it can be invasive, but good grief, Mr. Speaker, we should be able to do something! We usually have acess to only one French channel: Radio-Canada. And we had to fight for years to get that far. We succeeded when the federal Cabinet agreed to a policy of accelerated coverage in 1972-73. Since that time, we have had to fight every inch of the way to be able to continue to live and work in our own language.
Mr. Speaker, I don't think it is unreasonable to ask for as much as, but not less than what the others are getting.

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to begin debate on Bill C-158 on behalf of the Minister who could not be here today but who has a great deal of interest in this legislation.
This Bill is an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act to extend the variable entrance requirement, what we now call the VER. According to the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act, the person applying for unemployment insurance benefits must have a minimum of 14 weeks to qualify. Since the late 1970s, the VER has been used to make this requirement more flexible and responsive to the needs of unemployed Canadians, especially those who have been unable to accumulate more than 10 to 13 weeks of insurable employment to their credit.
The unemployment insurance program plays an important role in our social security system. Unemployment insurance benefits replace lost income. They help maintain the stability of local economies and also protect the jobs of people employed by those communities.

September 23, 1988
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
According to the VER, the number of weeks that an unemployment insurance claimant needs to qualify depends on the rate of unemployment in the region where he or she lives. Therefore, in regions of high unemployment claimants can qualify for unemployment insurance benefits with as few as 10 weeks of insurable employment.
As Hon. Members know, the present VER legislation is in effect only until January 3, 1989. We propose to renew it again in order to enable thousands of Canadians living in regions where the economy is not as strong as in other areas of the country to qualify for UI benefits. Despite the continuing decline in the unemployment rate since our coming to office we think that it would be beneficial at this time to maintain the protection provided by the VER.
Statistics show that the over-all Canadian economy is doing extremely well. Unfortunately, in some regions economic recovery is slower and the rate of unemployment remains higher than the national average. A failure to extend the variable entrance requirement at this time would have serious negative consequences for those regions.
One of the priorities of our Government is its desire to help those regions that are experiencing economic difficulty. The VER recognizes that it is more difficult to find and keep a job in a region of high unemployment. This is, in fact, one of the most important aspects of the UI program, since it takes into account the labour market conditions in each region of the country.
As the Minister announced on August 16, 1988, Employment and Immigration Canada is conducting a full review of the economic regions used to determine the minimum number of insurable weeks needed to qualify for benefits. We want to ensure that our system of economic regions is still responsive and sensitive to the changes that occurred as much in the distribution of people as in the employment opportunities in Canada.
If the VER is not renewed all claimants will, as of January 4, 1989, need at least 14 weeks of insurable employment to be entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. This means that more than 80,000 unemployed Canadians would be unable to meet the entrance requirements to receive UI benefits.
Thousands of Canadians would thus find themselves in difficulty, and most would have to turn to other sources to support themselves and their families. This would inevitably have an impact on provincial welfare programs. The Government wishes to continue to provide financial support to Canadians in designated regions, that is, those who need it the most.
It is important that Bill C-158, to renew the VER for a 12-month period, be passed as quickly as possible. In this way unemployment insurance claimants will know where they stand with regard to their entitlement.
As I mentioned earlier, the VER enables us to recognize economic disparity between regions when deciding the entitlement of UI claimants. It is in this connection that the
VER was created, and it is for this reason that we want to continue it for the next year.
I am asking for the support of all Members in passing this amendment for the renewal of the VER for a 12-month period until July 6, 1990.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Bill before us, Bill C-158, proposes to extend the period for variable entrance requirements, known as the VER, to January 6, 1990.
We will indeed support this legislation. The Government, of course, in its explanation was rather short and sweet. It is a simple Bill, I agree. It is not very complex. It proposes to extend the variable entrance requirement of the Unemployment Insurance Act and freeze the level of contributions for one year.
We all know that the variable entrance requirement provides that to qualify for unemployment insurance employees must work for 10 to 14 weeks and make contributions. They can qualify with 10 weeks of work if they live in a region where unemployment is over 9 per cent. The requirement increases from 10 weeks to 14 weeks when the rate of unemployment declines below 9 per cent. This provision is in recognition of the fact that in some parts of Canada it is very difficult to find work, which is why we provide in this legislation more unemployment insurance benefits in those regions.
I just looked up the figures a few minutes ago for the Ottawa-Hull area, and I want to put them on the record.
[ Translation]
The qualifying period for unemployment insurance in the Ottawa-Hull region is now 20 weeks for the first application. For the second application, it is from 14 to 20 weeks, depending on the number of weeks of benefits received as a result of the previous application. In the Ottawa-Hull area, the unemployment rate was 6.1 per cent in August 1988, compared to 7 per cent in August 1987. The number of people in the labour force in August 1988 was 443,000, compared to
419,000	last year. The number of unemployed was 29,000 in August 1988, compared to 32,000 in August 1987; nationally, the unemployment rate was 7.5 per cent in August 1988 and in Ontario, the rate for the whole province was 4.8 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, although we support this Bill, we regret that the Government has gotten into the habit of waiting nearly until the end of the session. Last time, it was just before Christmas. The day before the Christmas adjournment, or almost, the Government came to us in a mad rush with a Bill that it said had to be passed quickly. Today again, it is coming to us in a mad rush, and I am sorry that it is so, and telling us that this Bill must be passed. We agree. The Government could have called the Bill before to give Members and critics a chance to give the matter really serious consideration and to make suggestions to strengthen the provision whereby those who are out of work in Canada receive unemployment insurance.
September 23, 1988

We know that the unemployment rate has increased by about 0.1 per cent in Canada since last month. The main reason for the increased rate of unemployment was that 15,000 more people were looking for work in Canada; it was not due to an administrative change or a significant change in the level of employment or unemployment. The number of unemployed Canadians increased by 12,000 to 1,069,000, while the number of jobs throughout Canada increased by 3,000 to 12,367,000. This is despite some four years of economic growth. Indeed, 1 would say that the economic recovery began in 1983. This recovery is due to the growth in the world economy. The Government can claim that it is entirely responsible for this recovery, but I must say that it began before the Government took power in 1984. Furthermore, it is not confined to Canada; there is economic recovery throughout the world, in the United States, in Japan, in Europe. So that is not the reason.
The reason we have an economic recovery since 1984 is not the election of a Conservative Government. They were not there in 1983 or 1984. They took power in the fall of 1984, and God knows that since then, they have had a lot of luck and a lot of help from the world economic recovery.
And despite this sustained growth, the policies of the Mulroney Government have not reduced the unemployment rate below what it was before the 1982 recession. Even after six years of economic growth, we have not returned to the unemployment rate of before the 1982 recession. The average annual rate for 1980-81 was 7.5 per cent, which is not a seasonally adjusted figure. Job gains this month were recorded in Quebec with 13,000 and British Columbia with 4,000. The participation rate remained unchanged at 66.8 per cent. In addition, the proportion of the population with jobs also remained unchanged at 61.5 per cent. Compared to September 1984, the unemployment rate went down from 11.7 to 8 per cent, a drop of 3.7 points. The participation rate increased by 1.6 points, from 65.2 per cent in September 1984.
Mr. Speaker, the number of full-time jobs declined by
49,000	to 10,441,000, while the number of part-time jobs increased by 43,000 to 1,893,000.
As I said before, the situation in some regions of the country is disastrous! There are areas where the youth unemployment rate is 15 per cent. We must be concerned and aware of the difficulties these people face. And that is why there is a Bill before Parliament to amend or extend the Bill passed in 1976, if 1 am not mistaken, so that the period when the number of weeks that an insured person, other than a new entrant or reentrant to the labour force, shall have in order to qualify for benefits (based on the regional rate of unemployment) is extended until January 6, 1990.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to prolong the debate. I think that it is simple enough, but 1 would have preferred that the Government give us more notice and be more aware of the situation. But I think that many Members from the outlying regions hard-hit by unemployment would like to talk about

this Bill. So I will conclude my remarks with one final point. Mr. Speaker, the Government must not forget that it is important to review all of these social programs. subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to have an opportunity today to speak on behalf of my Party on Bill C-158. My colleague, the Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), had planned to speak on this when he anticipated that it was being brought forward on Tuesday of next week. As usual, the Government has not been able to follow through on its legislative agenda and, therefore, I get to fill in.
I am quite pleased, because 1 have been really upset about the Unemployment Insurance Act for quite some time. I should point out that we will be supporting this particular Bill because we recognize that, whatever else is wrong, at least in some areas it helps people in need.
The purpose of this Bill is to extend the variable entrance requirement, which has already been stated, and ensures in some areas of this country where there is higher unemployment than the national average, that people need only 10 weeks at the most to requalify.
It has a down side, too. Let me deal with the region that I come from, the region as defined by the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the Act. It is all of northwestern Ontario. The main community in that region is the City of Thunder Bay, which crosses two federal ridings, and then a lot of smaller communities, isolated hamlets of First Nations, spread throughout a very large area, an area that is larger than all of southern Ontario by many, many times. That is one region, for the purposes of this Act.
If you have a booming economy in Thunder Bay, the smaller communities, the outlying communities, need more and more weeks to requalify.
Let me use the example of the community of Atikokan. This is a community that now has a population of about 4,200 to 4,300. It used to employ 1,100 men mining iron ore. In 1979 and 1980, those mines shut down. The companies went in search of higher profits at other locations. But 1,100 jobs were wiped off the map. That community has been struggling since 1979 and 1980 to rebuild itself.

September 23, 1988
Through Canada Employment and Immigration and the local advisory committee for Atikokan, we did a study of that community. Because the community is so much smaller, we were able to go to every citizen to get a sense of their employment situation. What we discovered was that in 1987, one out of every two adults who were available for work were out of work for some point of time during that year. They did not get any benefit from Thunder Bay's booming economy. They were forced to adhere to the variable entrance requirements. As the economy in Thunder Bay improved, they needed more and more weeks to requalify. The same goes for Fort Frances, Kenora, Dryden and Ear Falls. Ear Falls is another community that saw a mine closing.
I was pleased to hear the speaker for the Government indicate that they are looking at those regions. If we are going to continue the variable entrance requirement-and I want to say something about that a little later-we should take a look at dealing with cities, not regions. We all know that there is almost full employment in Metropolitan Toronto. What does that say for other parts of Ontario that are part of that region? It means that those people are being punished because their neighbours are doing very well. That is also the underlying philosophy of the variable entrance requirement. The Government assumes-not just this Government, because this program was brought in by the previous one-that just because somebody else has been able to get a job, the person who is laid off will get one, too.
I see that you are indicating, Mr. Speaker, that my time at this point has run out. I want to give you notice that I will continue after we resume debate on this after Orders of the Day.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF REDRESS FOR JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) apologized to Japanese Canadians whom the Government of Canada mistreated during and after the Second World War. He also promised to pay $21,000 by way of redress to every living Japanese Canadian whom the Government relocated, interned and/or deported, expropriated, or otherwise deprived of the full enjoyment of his or her fundamental rights and freedoms simply because of his or her ancestry.
The Government will also clear the names of eligible Japanese Canadians who were convicted under the War Measures Act. It will also give $12 million to the Japanese Canadian community for educational, social, and cultural activities, and contribute $24 million toward the creation of a Canada Race Relations Foundation.

The Japanese Canadians whom I met with yesterday in Nepean-Carleton were shedding invisible tears of joy and pride. I, too, was proud, not only because of the outcome, but also because it was this Government that had the care and understanding to resolve a long-standing blemish on our history. Yesterday was a great day for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the contradictions and double-talk about what has gone on, and what is going on at the Defence Research Establishment, Suffield, are shocking.

September 23, 1988
The Minister of Defence (Mr. Beatty) has now admitted that lethal nerve gas tests took place at Suffield using both military personnel and civilians as guinea pigs. subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29(1) NERVE GAS TESTS AT CFB SUFFIELD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have today given notice to the Speaker of my intention to rise under the provisions of Standing Order 29 to seek leave to adjourn the House for the purpose of discussing a matter of urgent and pressing concern.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) has in the last several days acknowledged that an undetermined number of Canadians were subjected to nerve gas tests at the defence research establishment at Suffield, Alberta, particularly during but not limited to the 1960s.
Since the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) and I raised this issue several days ago we have received numerous calls from across the country from individuals who were subjected to such tests. In many instances these individuals are now suffering from medical disorders which may be directly related to these nerve gas tests.
The impact of such tests on the long-term health of the subjects has been well documented in other countries. I believe that it is absolutely vital that the federal Government conduct an open and public inquiry into this matter so that those subjects who were in fact exposed may be medically checked for any long-term effects.
An emergency debate in the House of Commons would serve that purpose in that it would further expose this issue in the public domain and thus assist those individuals who were or who may have been tested to come forward for immediate medical testing.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my comments on this Bill will be brief, since its purpose is simply to reconfirm certain rules that were established to allow Canadians in a number of peripheral regions who are experiencing hardship to have access to unemployment insurance. However, I would like to take this opportunity to point out that we still have no reply to our requests for applying the 10-week employment rule for unemployment insurance to our regions as well.
A number of Members, including myself, have asked to have certain parts of our ridings included among the regions that are eligible for unemployment insurance after only ten weeks. The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) said earlier that once again, the Government has waited until the very last minute to introduce this Bill. The Hon. Member knows perfectly well that Bill C-158 is one of those Bills that are introduced regularly on an annual basis and which do not contain any new elements. However, the request to allow certain areas in our ridings access to unemployment insurance after ten weeks of employment is new, and we are very anxious to see this done.
For instance, in the northern part of my riding, the communities of Notre-Dame-du-Laus, Poltimore and part of Val-des-Monts have a lot of unemployment, partly because of the sawmill that closed in the winter of 1984. To earn a living, these people have to leave home at five o'clock in the morning to get to work in Thurso. Mr. Speaker, you can imagine what this does to family life and the quality of life of these people?
I would also like to mention that in the 1987 report on the economy of Quebec published by Regional Industrial Expansion Canada, there is a very good description on page 93 of improvements in the economy of the Outaouais region. However, although there was a definite improvement in employment compared to 1986-an increase of 7.2 per cent- in 1986 this region was the only one where the number of persons holding a job decreased. When I say region, I am referring to the northern part of my riding and part of the riding next door, Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle, where the unemployment rate is above the national average.
Mr. Speaker, with these few words 1 just want to point out to the Minister that we absolutely must have a quick decision. For two years we have been waiting for a decision to include these areas among the regions where unemployment insurance is allowed after ten weeks. Of course, the answer would be to create jobs in these regions. In fact, we hope that as a result of the free trade agreement, the pulp and paper and forestry sectors, for instance, will expand very significantly, and we will thus be able to create jobs, which means that these people would no longer need unemployment insurance.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I want to thank my colleagues, both in the Opposition and in the Government, for their intervention. I appreciate the spirit of most of the people in this House.
When we broke at eleven o'clock, I was talking about the community of Atikokan and the difficulties that they have because of their location within the UI region of northwestern Ontario. I was pointing out that in 1987 one out of every two-in other words, 50 per cent of the employables in that community-were out of work for some period of time. Yet, because Thunder Bay's economy at that time was doing very well, they were forced to meet the same requirements as Thunder Bay in terms of the variable entrance requirements. Right now, that unemployment level is not much better in Atikokan. It is roughly between 8 and 9 per cent in Thunder Bay and the region, where they are required to have 17 weeks in order to requalify. That is a community that does not have the jobs to go around.
While we are hoping for a major announcement shortly due to some initiatives of the community, with the assistance of the federal and provincial Government, right now they are not benefiting in any way from Thunder Bay's prosperity, if I can put it that way, and they are being penalized for their location.
The other area that I am concerned about in terms of variable entrance requirements is based on two things. It is based on Statistics Canada's random sampling of the region, which again tends to be just Thunder Bay and which tends to be in the magnitude of 200 to 300 phone calls per month, which gives one a sense of the unemployment rates. Because of that sample size that we have seen in Thunder Bay, it is like a yo-yo. One month it is 12 per cent, the next month it is 8 per cent. It has been crazy.
They have fine tuned it by increasing the sample size a bit, but it still has a margin of error of 3.9. In other words, right now, when the unemployment rate is somewhere between 8 and 9 per cent, it could be 4 per cent or it could be 12 per cent. Yet, that is the statistic that determines the number of weeks that an individual is required to work in order to requalify.
The second part of that is that it is on a sliding average of over three months. As we saw this spring, fall and summer, because of the impact of the drought, in terms of the crops that were available to come through, plus some other distortions within the Western Grain Transportation Act, more and more railway workers, seafarers and grain handlers, as well as some government inspectors and weighers, were laid off. But that did not affect the unemployment rate fast enough to ensure that those who were laid off, who had been in a laid-off position previously and got called back to work, did not have enough weeks. They did not even have the 18 weeks that were then required. We have a situation where the system is not able to respond quickly enough.
I want to serve notice that when we get to report stage next week I want to move a couple of amendments to this Bill. One would in effect remove the variable entrance requirements and peg everybody at 10 weeks. I do not care whether you are a worker in Newfoundland, Yellowknife, Atikokan or Victoria, it does not mean that, just because your neighbour has been able to go out and get a job, you are automatically going to get one.
I am supporting this Bill because we do not want to see everybody get 14 weeks, because that will penalize those who obviously need the shorter qualifying period of 10 weeks that is provided for. Let us treat everybody equally with a ten-week qualifying period.
September 23, 1988

The other amendment 1 wish to give notice on will depend on what the Government does with my first amendment. If the Government does not accept the first amendment, I want to change it from a regional rate to a local rate, so that it is the unemployment rate in Thunder Bay, Corner Brook, or Saskatoon that decides the variable entrance requirements for that community, and not some larger piece of the pie where there may not be any relationship between employment and unemployment from community to community.
While I am speaking on the Bill, I would also like to make some general comments on unemployment insurance. During Question Period today I asked the Minister responsible for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer) if there was going to be assistance for the handlers of grain in any disaster program for the farmers. 1 pointed out to the Minister that some people are falling between the cracks. There are a number of grain handlers who have gone through three or four bad years of employment who cannot get 14, 15, 16, 17, or 18 weeks of work. We are finding that a number of them are being ruled ineligible to receive unemployment insurance on the basis of number of weeks. We are also finding that the rules of the game are making it even more difficult.
Currently, because of a mix up between Revenue Canada and the Unemployment Insurance Commission, vacation is treated differently. When an employee is off on scheduled vacation and is receiving payment from his or her employer, unemployment insurance continues to deduct the dues. However, Revenue Canada has ruled that vacation weeks cannot be counted, even though they are in the middle of the work period, and not at one end where they are used to perhaps circumvent the rules as they are today. Those employees are denied unemployment insurance benefits because they have been on paid holidays, which is part of their work, and part of a necessary component to ensure the mental and physical health of that employee. The system is not working on behalf of the people for whom it was designed. I would encourage the Government to make changes to it.
1 also wish to point out that an all-Party standing committee of the House unanimously recommended a ten-week qualifying period. That has also been recommended in some platform material and positions put forward by my Party.
My comments today are based on information from people who come into my constituency office in Thunder Bay or Atikokan. The bulk of our work is assisting people through the red tape of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. What happens to a laid off worker when he or she becomes sick is a real insult, particularly with respect to older workers. We have had cases where an individual on unemployment insurance, perhaps out of work for the first time in his or her life, has a heart attack. Many of these people who are in their early or late fifties obviously have extra stress when they are out of work. They are okay if they become sick in the first half of the claim period, but they do not dare get sick in the second half because they are cut off. That type of treatment of the unemployed has to stop.
Finally, we talk about the need to get people off unemployment insurance. I strongly believe that the vast majority of
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
men and women want to work. In some cases industries are shutting down. I mentioned the situation in Atikokan where the iron ore mines closed in 1979-1980. When people are laid off and are in an industry which has a declining workforce, either in their area or nationally, they know that they have to learn a new trade or develop a new skill. However, it cannot be done on unemployment insurance unless it involves one of that small group of programs under the Canadian Job Strategy that are specifically a seat purchase at a community college. There is no provision to allow someone to go to university to get his or her B.A. degree and move on to another skill area. If we really want to encourage people to get off unemployment insurance and into a full-time job, let us give them access to the educational system and allow them to claim unemployment insurance while they are going to school, for example, single parents, or mother-led families with the added burden of child care, who want to go to school to get an education.
One week ago I talked to a young woman who was attending Lakehead University. She told me that the Province of Ontario has cut her off in terms of her informal child care arrangement, because the budget was used up for the year. This woman is in her fourth year of university. One can imagine a single parent on welfare going to university because she knows that she needs the tools that education will provide her to get off welfare and be an employee in the community.
A number of things in the system need to be changed. I am pleased that I had an opportunity to contribute to the debate today. 1 hope that when the Bill is returned for report stage I will be present. These days one does not know when Bills will be returned, and even during the course of the day we are not sure. I hope to be here to move my amendments. If not, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), will move them on my behalf.
I appreciate your patience, Mr. Speaker, and I thank the Members in the House who allowed me to come back in, as it were. I regret that one Hon. Member saw fit to try to make life a little more miserable in this place.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to add to what the hon. gentleman has just said about the discrimination in vocational schools, in universities, and in all institutions of higher learning where there are some people who are collecting unemployment insurance and other people who are not collecting unemployment insurance. That is determined if one is in receipt of what one calls a "manpower seat". The Unemployment Insurance Commission, through the local employment office, determines that when a person is laid off it would be of benefit to that person to continue his or her education or go into a new field, therefore he or she is permitted to draw unemployment insurance.

September 23, 1988
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
In every province in Canada, starting in September in the vocational schools, when one goes into a typical classroom, one will find that one out of three or half the number of people are drawing unemployment insurance, and the other two-thirds or one-half are not. That is determined by whether or not you are acquainted with the system well enough to be able to, prior to your lay-off, go into the unemployment insurance office and get what is commonly referred to as a manpower seat.
Therefore, I agree with what the hon. gentlemen put on the record a few moments ago about the absolute and total discrimination of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Imagine the outrage people feel that Members of Parliament from the three political Parties sit in this Chamber and deal with the Act and have dealt with it over the years, yet we and the Senate do not agree on changing the system to make everyone equal. In fact, to put it on the record, perhaps most Members of Parliament and most Senators do not even know it is going on anyway.
Also for the record, this Bill before us today will continue what is commonly referred to as the variable entrance requirement. If the Bill does not pass what would it mean? The Bill affects only repeaters. It does not affect new entrants, or re-entrants as some Members have said. It does not affect how much unemployment insurance you get or who gets it. Not at all. What it affects is how many insurable weeks you need if you are a repeater.
You know what a repeater is. A repeater is a person who draws unemployment insurance consistently over 52 weeks. He re-enters the workforce and then applies for unemployment insurance. The variable entrance requirement comes into play depending on where you are in Canada, if you are a repeater and only if you are a repeater, not if you are what is referred to in the outrageous Act passed by this Parliament in 1978 and the outrageous Act that was passed by this Parliament in 1977 as a new entrant or a re-entrant. That has nothing to do with this Act. You can throw it in the garbage. It has to do with repeaters.
The Hon. Member stood up a few moments ago and said, my goodness, I am from the Outaouais, I believe it was, and she said, "We are longing for this Bill". If your unemployment insurance rate is fairly low and you are shouting for people to get unemployment insurance, then you had better vote against this Bill. You see, if the Bill is not passed, no matter where you were in Canada you would require 14 weeks of insurable employment to collect unemployment insurance, not 20 weeks as it is in a great many areas in Canada, nor 18 weeks, or 17 weeks, or 16 weeks, or 15 weeks. You would require 14 weeks right from Cape Spear, Newfoundland over to British Columbia. If you threw the Bill in the garbage, certain areas
of Canada would benefit, if you were supporting people to get unemployment insurance with fewer weeks required. Everybody would be the same. However, for the areas where presently you need only 10 weeks, up to 14 weeks, they would be required to get 14 weeks to collect unemployment insurance. That is what the Bill does. It does not do anything else.
Back in 1977 and 1978, as the present occupant of the chair will recall, this Chamber changed the law. Prior to 1977, as you will recall, you needed only eight weeks to collect unemployment insurance right across Canada. A Bill came in that changed that. That was followed by another Bill in 1978, and that Bill brought in the most discriminatory legislation that I have ever seen in this Chamber. We have lived with it ever since. I say today that what exists in the law today is outright and total discrimination. That is, a re-entrant to the workforce requires by law twice as many insurable weeks as a repeater.
In other words, what you find is this. In seasonal industries in northern Quebec, northern Ontario, northern British Columbia, the northern part of every province in Canada, in rural Canada, at a fish plant, for example, you will find on the working lines that a lady works maybe for three months, four months or five months of the year off and on during the summer. She gets maybe 1 5 weeks of insurable employment. When she is laid off, when she is no longer called back, she can collect unemployment insurance because she collected unemployment insurance the year before. However, next to her on the assembly line is another lady who, last year or the year before or the year previous to that, made the mistake of having a child. Then that lady is doomed forever never to qualify for unemployment insurance. Now, isn't that an outrageous thing to have in legislation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
It is there. I do not understand how Governments can come and go in this country and not correct that outright discrimination in the Unemployment Insurance Act. That lady who took a year out is now regarded by the law of Canada under the Act as a re-entrant into the workforce. Therefore, what does she require in Newfoundland? Twenty insurable weeks of employment within one year. You cannot space it out over two years.
The repeater with whom this Bill deals does not require 20 weeks by law passed by this Parliament. I suppose you could say that the same discrimination lies in our young people in Canada. They are not affected by this Bill either because they are what you call new entrants. New entrants are classified the same way as that lady who took one year out to have a child. They also require five months of insurable employment in order to be a new entrant as defined under the Act.
September 23, 1988

The real things that are wrong with the Act that revolve around this legislation called the variable entrance requirement are the things that should change. In fact, I just wonder which political party will try to set the record straight in the election and have as part of its platform the removal of that discrimination under the Act. I do not know of any political party as yet that has adopted that policy. What political party is going to turn around and correct a grave injustice in this country?
If we use the example of the fish plant worker in Canada drawing unemployment insurance, this woman with 15 weeks can draw it but another woman cannot because she took a year out. As you know, it has been a bad fishery in eastern Canada. Why is it that the fishermen of Canada cannot collect unemployment insurance? If a fisherman has 10 weeks, 20 weeks, 30 weeks, 40 weeks, 50 weeks, 60 weeks or even 1,000 weeks, he cannot draw unemployment insurance today. It is not allowed.
This Parliament, in its infinite wisdom, passed a law that said that a fisherman could only draw unemployment insurance commencing November 15, the time when he could file, and he would get his first cheque on December 12, and his last cheque would, by law, be limited to May 10. That is obviously discrimination. One fish plant worker is collecting unemployment insurance because he has 12 weeks or 15 weeks. Another fish plant worker, a lady who had a child two years ago, cannot collect it because she had a child two years ago and had to take the year off. In order to re-enter, she now requires 20 weeks. The fisherman who brings in the fish cannot collect unemployment insurance at all until the middle of November. He then has to file for it and wait for two weeks.
In fact, most fishermen wait more than two weeks. A fisherman filing in Grand Falls, Newfoundland, which is not as yet in my riding, would have to wait eight weeks. The eight-week rule is that if he quits, he cannot get the benefits for eight weeks, six weeks of penalty and two weeks of waiting time. They are so overworked and understaffed in some of those unemployment insurance offices that the fisherman files but all he gets are forms in the mail.
What political party will have the wisdom, the common sense and the sense of fair play to tell Canadians that it will right all the wrongs in the Act? What Government will do what the courts of Canada have started to do? There have been some decisions lately by the Federal Court of Appeal including a recent one dealing with the spouses' aspect of the Unemployment Insurance Act. There have been two cases overruling that section of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
People are asking why parliamentarians cannot right the wrongs in the Act. They are asking why they have to go through these appeal procedures and end up not winning when they know that there is discrimination in the Unemployment Insurance Act.
1 intended to say only a few words about the trade school students to whom the Hon. Member referred a few moments
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
ago. Again, there is discrimination in the Unemployment Insurance Act. Half a trade school class in carpentry is allowed to collect unemployment insurance and the other half cannot. Half a secretarial class at a trade school is allowed to collect unemployment insurance but the other half is not. One person is collecting unemployment insurance but the person sitting next to him in class who did the same job and has the same history is not allowed to draw unemployment insurance. That is discrimination, is it not? Any court would say that that is outright discrimination under any charter of rights.

September 23, 1988

Mr. Chairman, the Member for Thunder Bay- Atikokan did provide the Official Opposition with a copy of the amendment to Bill C-158. I wish to indicate that the Official Opposition supports the amendment proposed by the New Democratic Party. The Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, which examined the whole question of unemployment insurance entitlements, recommended unanimously, that is, members from all three Parties, Conservative, Liberal and the third Party in the House, the New Democratic Party, that such an amendment be made to the Act and that the qualification criteria for benefits be applied equally across the country. But what we do not see today in this Bill, unfortunately, is a requirement to get rid of the 20-week rule for re-entrance.
I represent a riding where unemployment is among the highest in the country. For example, in the Port au Port Peninsula the unemployment rate is between 50 per cent and 60 per cent, even during the height of the fishing season. It is ridiculous that someone who managed to get a job last year and is going back to the same seasonal job this year, needs 10 weeks to qualify for unemployment insurance purposes, but someone who was so unfortunate as not to get a job last year, one of the ones who are not employable, not for lack of trying but merely because of lack of opportunity, needs 20 weeks.
What could be more insane than asking the workforce who lives in that part of Canada where their way of life depends upon seasonal economies, be it the fishery, the forestry or certain agricultural sectors, to wait 20 weeks? What could be more ludicrous than saying that those who seasonally find employment to give to themselves and their families the dignity of a pay cheque, can qualify after 10 weeks of employments, but those who fall between the cracks, those who are required to go out and scrape, to almost beg or steal, to find enough income to make it through the summer months and into the fall, must wait 20 weeks? Because they had a bad year, they did not qualify in one year, so the next time, in order to qualify, they are required to have 20 weeks of employment.
1 would have hoped the Government, paying attention in a reformed Parliament to the progressive and enlightened views of Members from all three Parties on the standing committee operating in a non-partisan manner and seeking to make better laws for all Canadians, would have come in with a Bill to get rid of the variable entrance requirement and make it ten weeks across the country.
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
The reality is that anybody who can work beyond ten weeks will work. I do not know anyone who does not want to work. There may be a rare case, but one cannot build a law for the country based on a rare case. People whom I know want the dignity of a day's work, the pride that comes with bringing home a paycheque. This nonsense that we need a variable entrance requirement because the country, en masse, is going to lay down its tools and go home now that they have qualified is nonsense.
There is a work ethic that ought to be reflected in faith in the working people of this country by the Government of Canada bringing in an universal 10-week requirement and getting rid of the terrible discriminatory 20-week re-entrance requirement. Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have been in this position in Committee of the Whole. I have been on the other side for a few hours in this Chamber over the years.
Close to 20 years ago I became involved in doing research work across this country related to employment concerns from coast to coast, Newfoundland included. I would like to confirm my hon. friend's observation that Canadians want to work. They want to work productively; they are hard-working people. We have no reason to be afraid of a free trade deal because our people will make it work and the opportunities will enable them to have the jobs.
We do have arguments about the best way to provide jobs. I remember the arguments in 1984. We brought in our first Budget and opposition Members, who came to that budget process like they had come to four years of governing, said that it would be a catastrophe, that our unemployment insurance fund would be bankrupted because there would be so many unemployed people. Four years later there are 1.25 million more Canadians who pay money into the unemployment insurance fund, and there are a whole lot less people who take money out.
Voters will have a chance to decide which Party's view is the most appropriate one. We offer four years of experience of creating jobs and reducing the costs of unemployment insurance versus the preceding four years when jobs disappeared and unemployment insurance payments went up. We believe that Canadians who want jobs will vote for us, and we believe that that is the overwhelming majority of Canadians.
On the amendment, the research data shows that beginning at about 12 weeks and going up to 20 weeks and beyond is probably the best statistical definition of the Canadian labour force. If people do not, by and large, have that kind of attachment-not in every single year, but through the passage of time-it is hard, in a statistical sense, to say that they are part of the labour force. It is important to have other social programs that look after their economic needs when they are not part of the labour force, and we do have such programs.

September 23, 1988
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
However, the Unemployment Insurance Act compels people to put money. Every employee in the country on a wage must put money in. It is a tax, kind of a hidden tax in a way, but people do not have an option. They must put money in and the money that comes in is topped up by government, but it has to match the money that is paid out.
If we try to meet all our social needs, all our income needs for things like the welfare system under the Canada Assistance Plan, through unemployment insurance, then we would have to tell the employees of the country that they have to put more money in, that we are going to tax them higher. We would have to tell the businesses of the country that we are going to have to tax them higher to pay for that.
Any tax on labour should be entered into very carefully because it is a carrot to business to discontinue with a job, to replace a job with a machine. That is what a tax on labour does, and if we are really concerned about those Canadians who want jobs then we really have to be careful. The Opposition has put forward, and both Parties seem in agreement on this, an increase in taxation for those who have jobs.
The Member opposite raises the standing committee report. At the point at which that report was brought to Parliament, I was the chairman of the committee so I think I indeed know an awful lot about that report. It bothers me that some days in the House of Commons the report is distorted.
Members worked very hard with the resources we had. The hours, the days, and the weeks went by and we proposed a major restructuring of the unemployment insurance principle. We did not have the resources to do all the research, but we believed that it would produce better benefits at lower taxation.
When we pull a single recommendation out of the over 50 recommendations we are not treating the Act as a whole, as a total arrangement. This amendment is simply proposing an increase in taxation for people. That is really what is being proposed, whereas the Bill that the Government has brought in is saying that in areas where jobs are not available, where it is very difficult to get more than ten weeks of work, one shall qualify. However, if one lives in an area like downtown Toronto or southwestern Ontario where there is almost a labour shortage today, where jobs are readily available, one has to work longer, because jobs are there, to get one's pay.
It is the Government's view that those who really need the help because they come from an area where jobs are hard to get shall benefit under unemployment insurance, but we do not want those same people to pay the costs of people who come from downtown Toronto where jobs are readily available.
That is the reason for variable entrance. We do not want to tax the poor to pay the rich. This amendment would force us to tax the people from high unemployment areas higher to pay benefits in downtown Toronto. We think it should work the other way, that those coming from areas where jobs are readily
available should pay more to help Canadians in other parts of the country where jobs are very difficult to get.
I would urge government Members to vote against this amendment for those reasons.

1 would point out to him, among other things, that to generalize like that may not in fact make sense. I have walked along Bloor Street in Toronto where there are signs offering jobs. 1 have walked in areas of my constituency where there are signs in retail stores offering jobs.

I do not know of anybody who can live on fresh air or water if one has any water-and some communities do not have any water to drink.
Someone might say that that person could go to welfare. If one goes to welfare one might end up in jail. What does one do if one qualifies for unemployment insurance and one goes to to welfare? The first thing one has to do is one must sign a form. One says in that form that when one receives one's unemployment insurance the welfare department will be paid back what has been received. Then one signs another form that states that in accepting the money from welfare-I call it welfare, it is social assistance in some places, I suppose, but welfare is the term that we know on the coastline of Newfoundland-one may now be guilty of neglect if one has a family or people to support because one has quit one's job.

For those people who draw the maximum unemployment insurance, they run the risk in December of having to pay it back. Why? Somebody said to me one day: "You know what is wrong with the Unemployment Insurance Commission. A fellow goes out and makes $70,000 a year and then goes on unemployment insurance. He makes that during the winter and goes on unemployment insurance for the rest of the summer". That is not right. As you know, there is a law that says that there is a maximum one can make from one's total income for the year plus one's unemployment insurance. If one makes any more, one has to pay back the unemployment insurance. It is on one's income tax form.
Somebody who fills out income tax and claims unemployment insurance benefits knows what I am talking about. Some people who do not collect unemployment insurance, like Members of Parliament, do not know what I am talking about. But one fills it out. That maximum level is monitored by Revenue Canada.
How many cases do we have in Canada of school teachers who lose their jobs, are supposedly qualified for unemployment insurance, but at the end of the year, December 31, when they
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
do their income tax for that year they find that they have gone over $40,000 in total income, that is, from their work plus unemployment insurance. National Revenue governs this. What happens? They have to pay back their unemployment insurance to the Department of National Revenue.
We have these checks and balances within the Unemployment Insurance Act if one tries to collect the maximum on unemployment insurance which, as we proved a moment ago, is about $340 a week. Boy, what a fortune that is, that is, if one claims the maximum. One runs the risk of having to pay it back to the Department of National Revenue at the end of the year because one was in a high paying job prior to that.
What is the average? What do people make on average in unemployment insurance throughout Canada? What is the average cheque that we would find in the area of the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe with the inshore fishermen? An additional 10 per cent is knocked off the 60 per cent if he owns a boat. Anyway, that is another story. We will find that it averages to about $150 a week. One may say: "Well, $150 a week, boy, he might quit his job and go on unemployment insurance".
The average man collecting unemployment insurance in the riding of the Hon. Member to my left would receive about the same as he would receive from welfare if he quit his job and went on unemployment insurance. That is the truth of the matter.
Since the Government of Canada took office four years ago, it cut out the mobility grants. It cut them out,
You just cannot get a job where you are after you get laid off.

speechtext: If you are broke, you cannot move.

Last Tuesday, the Government of Canada sent out letters to all those air traffic controllers who were fired in the United States in 1981, offering them jobs in Canada. Mobility is totally paid for. On the job training allowance for eight months is over $ 1,000 a week.

Perhaps we should raise it in Question Period at the beginning of the week and ask the Government of Canada, through the Minister of Employment and Immigration who sponsors this Bill, why on the one hand it signed a piece of paper overruling the Immigration Department's guidelines on the employment of federal public servants and on the other hand approved mobility money for the movement of U.S. air traffic controllers who were fired in 1981 to fill jobs across Canada. There are 45 of them going to Pearson International Airport. That is the double standard we get.

September 23, 1988

What a change there has been for a person who draws unemployment insurance being able to land a job like they have now offered to the Americans, all those air traffic controllers, so that they can come in and fill the best jobs we have in Transport Canada, the best jobs from the point of view of money, because they are very high pressure jobs.
A lot of Canadians just wanted to write the exams for entrance to air traffic control. They are going to be surprised to learn that the Americans are being offered those jobs automatically and getting over $1,000 a week for on the job training.
What I was trying to say is that when one is looking for a job and is on unemployment insurance, one has a more distressing problem today than one had over four years ago, because the Department of manpower or the employment Department sponsoring this Bill no longer keeps records of people in manpower offices. The records are no longer kept. There is no longer a computer.
One used to be able to go in, prior to the entrance of the present Government, and register. A fellow would keep one on file and if something came up, one got a phone call. There is no more registration of a general worker who gets laid off. They do not keep all those files because the Government of Canada said that there were no jobs around. Perhaps we should not keep the files.
When we once talked about going down to register at the manpower office, that used to be the call. "Let's go down and register at the manpower office". Well, there is no such thing any more. One cannot do it. In fact, it used to be interesting, because one was either actively looking for work, where one came in every three months, or one was on the less than active file. There are no more files.
Even for the federal employment programs that hire people drawing unemployment insurance the call is: "Do you want a job? Listen to the radio. If you are not listening to the radio when the jobs are advertised, then you cannot get a job because for the 10 workers that were advertised at two minutes after one o'clock on radio station CKGA, we have already had 10 phone calls or 100. We take the first 10". Consequently, if there is a job for a captain of a ship on an ice-breaker up North, a fellow might be sitting at home who was not listening to the radio. He might have been a captain for 22 years and had the best record on the Atlantic Ocean. However, he was not listening to the radio. There may be another guy who perhaps did not have enough experience but was able to hop in and get the job because he was listening to the radio.
The entire system has changed and because of that system we now need a total revision of the Unemployment Insurance Act. It cannot be picked at or dealt with by bringing in a Bill such as the one we are dealing with today. I do not disagree with the Bill. However, it only deals with repeaters. It does not
deal with new entrants or re-entrants. It does not deal with anything but repeaters. It deals with the status quo.
In the interim the mobility grants have been removed so that someone cannot go from point A to point B. Perhaps someone tells an unemployed fellow down in Bay St. George in Newfoundland that there are lots of jobs in Toronto and in southern Ontario doing drywall. Do you know what drywall is, Mr. Chairman? It is gyprocking. Then the fellow says: How am I going to get up there? I can't get mobility any more".
The Government so restricted mobility that under the new rules a person has to prove that he or she has a job that is guaranteed for over one year. The employer must also advertise locally for six months, and the employer has to guarantee a job for one year before the Government will pay up. How is a person supposed to get money to go to Toronto if he or she is poor, does not have any money, and his or her family does not have any money? I suppose he or she could hitch-hike, but that is kind of difficult.
When the person reaches Toronto there is an additional problem. If the person wants to stay anywhere, he or she has to put down a downpayment on accommodation. Just imagine someone making $120 week on unemployment insurance trying to keep the family going, hitch-hiking all the way up there, and then being told that a month or two month's rent in advance is needed.
The Department of Employment and Immigration no longer keeps any records to refer a person to the job that she or she is best suited for. That was changed when the present Government took over. There are no longer mobility grants available to go for a job search. That has all been changed. When the system is changed so completely, it has to be counterbalanced and some attempt made at taking care of the people who are being hurt by the system. That is why I would support any of those measures mentioned by the hon. gentleman.

Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan is the appropriate one, given that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister and the President of the Privy Council has said that the Government is in accord, at least with the spirit or the intent of the amendment that the entrance rate be determined by circumstances in the local region.
