It is more than a good wish, a goodwill, or a desire, but it is spelled out in the Act as now drafted.
There is another area which the Government, between now and third reading if it chooses, could address to remove a major piece of discrimination in this Bill. There is only one group of people in Canada who have a special set of requirements that apply to them based on the definition of their work. Every other worker in Canada qualifies or is disqualified for unemployment insurance based on a variable entrance requirement, and the rules that apply throughout the Act apply to every working person in Canada. However, there is one group of workers who have a set of rules designed only for them. That group of workers is fishermen. Only fishermen have a clause in the Unemployment Insurance Act tailor-made for them.

September 23, 1988
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
Canadians watching could be saying to themselves: "What a fortunate group of people these fishermen are, a special clause just for them. My gosh, they are well represented in the Elouse of Commons in that they were able to cause such a tremendous feat to occur that they have special rules just for fishermen".
What is this special rule? It is a rule which says that a fishermen cannot qualify, cannot receive, cannot be paid, cannot cash an unemployment insurance cheque between May 15 and November 15. No fisherman in Canada for that period of time, six months, between May 15 and November 15, can receive an unemployment insurance cheque. Why? It is because fishermen are supposed to be fishing between that time.
It is a perfectly logical, rational rule brought in by a previous Liberal Government and maintained by the current Conservative Government. It was well intentioned but it no longer works in some areas. I represent the great northern peninsula of Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: That is their problem.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
It is a problem for the Government, of that there is no doubt. Members can laugh, but on the great northern peninsula of Newfoundland we will find some of the hardest working, heartiest, dedicated people with the biggest amount of pride and dignity in their belly. They manage to scrape out a living, and a decent one, in difficult circumstances, clinging on by their fingernails to the rocks at the edge of the salt water, harvesting the resource of the sea. Proud people, proud to go out and work when they can, while they can, in every kind of circumstance, overcoming every kind of difficulty.
Yet there is one thing they cannot overcome with this rule that says they cannot collect unemployment insurance from May to November. They cannot overcome the fact that some 14 feet of ice does not melt on the great northern peninsula until July. Yes, throughout the winter, right straight through until the middle of July some years, can find ice rafted up in the harbours, barring the boats, and on the land right into July. Yet the rule says that by May 15 they should be fishing. Therefore, on May 15 there is no more unemployment insurance. From May 15 through June 15 to July 15, two months, there is no income. Why? It is because some lad in Ottawa sitting in his ivory tower, with his coffee cup and his pack of butts, perhaps with his feet on his desk and his central air-conditioning on, contemplating lunch with his buddy down the hallway in the subsidized cafeteria, said that Genge or Anchor Point is supposed to be out fishing so, damn it, let them fish.
They cannot fish. It is physically impossible. There is ice as high as the gilded roof of this glorious chamber on their front doorsteps, their boats are barred in, but some bureaucrat has said they have got to be fishing. It is impossible, so every year from May until July these fishermen, year in and year out, are penalized. They are discriminated against because they cannot go fishing. In the interim they cannot receive an income.
That is only half the story. There is another problem. This time of the year, September 23, you can do down to Dow's Lake on a Saturday with your sweater on, if you have a good day you can do down in your bikini, and watch the pretty boats sail around. It is a wonderful day. However, on September 23, if you are in Port au Choix, in St. Anthony, Quirpon, or if you are in Anchor Point, Flower's Cove, Savage Cove, Sandy Cove, or Bear Cove, you are not going down to the water to watch the pretty sailboats in your sweater or maybe your bikini. No, we have another problem, invented by God. It is called weather, fall weather.
We have the fact of no fish because the fish migrate. God invented that as well. He set up a migratory pattern and the fish move in and the fish move out and at a certain time of the year they move off again. Also at a certain time of the year, the fall and winter weather begins. Anyone who does not live there does not know what happens on the North Atlantic. They have no concept of what it is like to be in a small boat at sea at that time of the year. From September until November 14 these Fishermen cannot fish either. There is a six-month period in which they cannot qualify because they are supposed to be fishing. For three of the six months they cannot fish. It is not because they do not want to fish, nor because they are not prepared to fish, nor because they do not have every desire to be out so they can have the dignity of a paycheque. It is because it is physically impossible.
What does the Parliament of Canada say as it brings in Bill C-158 to those fishermen from the great northern peninsula or the other Atlantic provinces in similar circumstances? There are some regions where the fishery is a winter fishery and not much is done at all during the summer season. Do we say "let us invent an Act that has a variable zone recognition like we have a variable entrance requirement recognizing this fact of life, this creation of God, this planet earth where not all things are consistent"? No, that does not happen. What we have every year is the status quo. Every year the fishermen are told that we will take a look at it next year. Every year the civil servant, whoever he is, who advises that faceless, nameless Minister, puts his feet back on his desk, once again sucks back deep on his coffee cup, thinks once again about his meal over at Hy's restaurant, his expense paid lunch, and says: "We will get around to it next year".
Let this be the last year that this Parliament, in the splendid comforts of these felt covered chairs, these great stained glass windows, these hunks of marble, sits here in comfort and forgets the plight of hardworking fishermen on the great northern peninsula of Newfoundland who want nothing more than a fair shake. They want, for once, these people who draft their Bills on the edge of the Rideau to think about those people who live on the edge of the Strait of Belle Isle, who work hard for a living, and want nothing but a fair shake from the Parliament of Canada.

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   SOCIAL SERVICES OVERPAYMENTS TO BENEFICIARIES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of prohibiting any federal department or agency which has in error made an overpayment to an individual under a social program from claiming repayment or withholding the overpayment from future payments to the individual, unless the individual is responsible directly or indirectly for the error.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise to deal with what many Canadians will think is a small injustice, but it is an injustice nonetheless. What attracts me to it is that it is an injustice from which poor people in Canadian society suffer more than others.
The matter came to my attention through the coincidence of three constituents coming to me with exactly the same type of problem. They were living on the benefits of one government program or another. In the case of all three, they were veterans living on veterans' pensions. Because of a computer error made in Prince Edward Island, 1 suppose, because that is where the administration of the veterans' pensions is, they received overpayments for, in one case, a year and a half.
During that period of time these people received more money than they were entitled to under a government program, but not a lot more. They were not in a position to confirm the exact amount of money they should have been getting. They simply received cheques, took them to the bank, and lived on the amount of money they were getting. In one of the three cases there was no other source of income for the family. It was the entire income of an elderly couple.
Social Services
It turned out in these three cases, and as my investigations have shown in hundreds and hundreds of other cases across Canada, that a computer error had occurred. The computer was not wrong; it was human error, but it is an understandable error that can occur in a government department.
After the mistakes were discovered, the Government got in touch with these people and told them that they had received overpayments and that their subsequent payments would be reduced while the Government paid itself back for the excess amount it had paid out. It creates a very great hardship for people who find themselves in that situation. It is not that they were entitled to the overpayment. They were not entitled to it, but they were unaware of it.
When the time came for their payments to be reduced, it was extremely difficult for these people to adjust. They wrote to me as their Member of Parliament and I got in touch in one case with the Ministry of Veterans Affairs and in another case with the Ministry of Employment and Immigration. The Ministries feel that their hands are tied and that they have no recourse but to recuperate the overpayment. That is why I am inviting my colleagues on all sides of the House to pass a resolution to give some guidance to the Government in cases like this.
Unfair is perhaps not the exact word for this kind of circumstance, but it is very unfortunate and it is also a circumstance which is in no way the fault of the people involved. They were the beneficiaries of an overpayment, but as Hon. Members will see from the language that I have used in my resolution, an important factor in not reclaiming payment is that the recipients not be at fault.
In other words, I am not addressing the situation of the recipients of overpayments giving wrong information to the Government or, as happens in a lot of other cases that are very regrettable, failing to reveal that they have jobs and are collecting unemployment insurance at the same time, and then down the road, someone learning about it and the unemployment insurance payments have to be paid back along with interest and in some cases penalties. I am addressing in this resolution only situations in which it is wholly the Government's fault that people received overpayments in the first place. In cases like that, they ought to be allowed to keep these usually very modest overpayments.
I will not speak a long time on this motion. It is a simple idea and I do not think it takes an a lot of explanation, but I would like to indicate that when I raised this matter before the parliamentary committee that considers these matters, committee members asked a very good question.

They asked me how such a situation would be handled, say where someone receives a payment that is a million dollars more than what was sought. I admit that can happen!

September 23, 1988
Social Services
We often read in the newspapers of people who got something like $10 million instead of $10 from some government department, 1 am ready to admit that this must be considered.
If the Government is prepared to accept the motion, and if the Members of the House accept it, setting limits of say 15 or 20 per cent in excess, I would be very grateful for such a policy.
1 do not want... I am not suggesting that if a public servant gives a citizen one million dollars too much, that person should keep it. We can imagine conspiracies, situations where a government official wanting to help someone could have the computer make a mistake and give the individual in question a million-dollar overpayment. One can ask whether it would be fair to keep that money. This is not what I am talking about.
1 ask Members who will speak to consider the situations they no doubt know of in their ridings, like cases where people have received overpayments that the Government wants back.
By setting reasonable limits, we can control extreme cases. [English]
I do not want to write a blueprint for getting super windfalls when the decimal point is five or six digits out of line. I am only referring to the very real and increasingly frequent situation of a modest overpayment over a prolonged period of time, resulting in a really tough time for elderly poor people who rely on government payments, did not know the amount was excessive, and are suddenly forced to live with an important amount of money less than they were getting before. I think that is the kind of situation that my resolution is meant to address. I hope that Hon. Members will support it, that it will pass, and that the Government will adopt it as a policy within the range of a certain margin of error.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   SOCIAL SERVICES OVERPAYMENTS TO BENEFICIARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to Motion No. 167, let me begin by thanking the Hon. Member for raising the matter of overpayment to an individual under a government program and for providing an opportunity for the House to debate the issue.
The Government is of course very aware of the importance of its social programs and the concerns expressed by the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) about the recovery of overpayments. It has been and continues to be the practice of this Government to deal with such matters with compassion and understanding. To this end, the Government, in 1986, included specific statutory provisions authorizing the remission of overpayments resulting from administrative error in program legislation such as the Canada Pension Plan, the Old Age Security Act, the Family Allowances Act, and the War Veterans Allowance Act.
Section 65(3) of the Canada Pension Plan, which is typical of such provisions, provides that the Minister may remit all or any portion of an overpayment on any one of four grounds, and I quote:
The amount... cannot be collected within the reasonable foreseeable future.
The administrative costs of collecting the amount or excess of the allowance are likely to equal or exceed the amount to be collected.
Repayment of the amount or excess of the allowance would cause undue
hardship to the person or institution, or
The amount or excess of the allowance is the result of erroneous advice or
administrative error on the part of an official of the Department.
During the last fiscal year over 11,000 overpayments were written off under these provisions. Furthermore, in the event that an unforeseen situation arises for which no specific provision has been enacted, the Minister concerned can turn to the regulations made pursuant to Section 18 of the Financial Administration Act which provides for the writing off of debts as uncollectable on grounds of hardship.
From what I have just outlined, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the necessary legislative authorities are in place for a compassionate implementation of the recovery of overpayments. The Government will, of course, continue to monitor the situation as part of its ongoing regular review of program delivery and will make any statutory adjustments that may be required as the needs arise.
I would like to point out that what may appear to be an administrative error may in fact be a deliberate strategy aimed at ensuring continuity of payment. The Government is acutely aware of the need for Canadians on fixed incomes to be assured that they will receive their payments regularly and without interruption. Cheques are, therefore, often prepared in advance, on the basis of expected entitlements and adjusted later, if necessary. This practice does not normally present major financial difficulties when the adjustment is made immediately, that is, on the subsequent payment.
However, as 1 am sure you can understand, Mr. Speaker, the alternative of verifying entitlement before each and every payment is just not practical for all programs. First, it would cause delays while the Department concerned waited for the benefit recipient to file the necessary information. Second, it would create an additional administrative burden for both the recipient and the Department and would result in a waste of resources which could better be used to process new applications and improve service to the program recipients.
In some cases, entitlements may be scheduled to be adjusted quarterly, semi-annually, or even only annually. Because of changes in a recipient's status in the intervening period, entitlement and hence the payment may be reduced on the next scheduled adjustment date. However, the higher amount received during the previous period should not be classified as an overpayment, but the amount to which the individual was entitled during that period. Nor is the subsequent reduction a recovery, but merely a reflection of the revised entitlement.
This House should also bear in mind that in the case of general programs like the Canada Pension Plan and family allowances, not all recipients are living on a limited income. To remit automatically all overpayments, even where recovery would not cause hardship, would be unfair not only to all taxpayers in general, but more important, to the other program recipients who would not receive the same "windfall".
I maintain that the current system which allows Ministers to remit overpayments on a case by case or class basis provides a reasonable balance between equity and compassion.
September 23, 1988

Finally, the Government is continuing to take action to improve the accuracy and response time of the complex and automated systems used to deliver benefits. For example, the Department of Veterans Affairs has just completed the implementation phase of a major overhaul of its benefit delivery systems. The Department of National Health and Welfare has embarked on a similar exercise. Such improvements, of course, must be done in such a manner as to respect the dignity of the individual as well as the provisions of the Privacy Act. Otherwise, 1 am sure that the Hon. Member for York Centre would be among the first to complain about government intrusion and data matching.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to participate in the debate today on the motion put forward in the name of the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan). 1 want to compliment and thank him for bringing the motion forward. It is an important issue.
When I called my constituency office in Thunder Bay to update my memory in terms of work we have done in this area, my constituency assistant, Rosemary Cox, was quite excited about the motion because it is an area with which she has to deal quite frequently. She gave me examples of three areas where we have had problems, but they are only a reflection of many problems because, as Hon. Members know, the constituency offices which are provided to us by Parliament are there to help our citizens work through some of their problems with government bureaucracy. We are really the one focal point they have to find out how they can appeal what has been done to them.
I have found that all the problems centre around people who have very small incomes. Whether it is unemployment insurance, veteran's allowance, Canada Pension Plan, or old age security with the income supplement, by and large we are talking about men and women who do not have that much money.
Therefore, we are talking about people who, when asked to make a repayment for whatever reason, have great difficulty in doing so. They can and they do make those repayments, but it means their meagre income for that repayment period is reduced. Even if it is only $10 a month that is agreed to for a repayment plan, it has an impact on a senior who only has the old age pension with the income supplement. It is important that we highlight this problem. Hopefully, the House will send a direction to the Government, as suggested by the Hon. Member for York Centre in terms of the motion. The motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of prohibiting any federal department or agency which has in error made an overpayment to an individual under a social program from claiming repayment or withholding the overpayment from future payments to the individual, unless the individual is responsible directly or indirectly for the error.
We have had a number of such cases with the Canada Pension Plan where through no fault of their own but through some bureaucratic mix-up seniors have received more money than they were entitled to. There was no fraud or attempt to
Social Services
beat the system. Someone along the line pushed the wrong button in the computer or misread the regulations and the pensioner received an overpayment. The Government then came, as is its responsibility, and said "I am sorry, you were overpaid. We have to get that money back".
In some cases they are able to negotiate with the individuals to find a repayment scheme that is acceptable to them, that is within their financial means to handle. Other times, and again through the same kind of bureaucratic snafu, all of a sudden the cheques stop coming and that creates a panic because they rely on them.
Under old age security with the income supplement, because it is based on your over-all income, in some cases there is retroactivity. You find when you fill out your income tax form that you goofed on your projection, that you actually made a couple hundred dollars more than you told the Government you were going to when you applied for your income supplement. The Government sees this and matches it with its other records, decides it overpaid you, and wants the money back. These are, again, people with meagre incomes.
We had one case where the Unemployment Insurance Commission ruled that an individual was eligible to receive unemployment insurance benefits. That individual received them for one full year and, lo and behold, Revenue Canada decided that unemployment insurance had made a mistake, that this individual was not eligible. It demanded full repayment of a full year's worth of unemployment insurance benefits.
The final example I want to use is a program called Futures developed by the Province of Ontario. It was designed as a youth employment training program to provide a combination of classroom studies, life skills, how to do resumes, and how to dress for an interview, plus some on the job work experience.
At the start of the program the students involved applied for unemployment insurance and were told that this program was eligible, that they would be able to count every week in this program because they were getting paid by the Province of Ontario to be trained to get a job. They were told that every week they were in this program would be counted as a UI week.
Later, after the program was over, the rules changed. I do not know whether it was somebody higher up in UI, but they decided that only the time spent at the on the job training was eligible for UI. These young people were making minimum wage and would not have received all that much in any case because, as we know, the level of unemployment insurance benefits is based on earnings. In effect they would be getting less than minimum wage in UI benefits. They were told that they had to repay almost half of what they received from unemployment insurance. That is not exactly a good way to introduce them to the working world, is it?

September 23, 1988
Social Services
There are hundreds of examples out there. If Members just talk to their constituency assistants I am sure they can all provide examples. This motion does not say how to do it, and I recognize that there is some ministerial discretion. That is tied up, too, in the bureaucracy, and getting to that level takes time. These people do not have time.
Our seniors, the people who built this country, really get upset when somebody in authority comes knocking at the door saying that they owe the Government money. It makes them feel as if they they did something wrong, that instead of being the victims they were the perpetrators. I think it is important that we give them the benefit of the doubt. The former Minister of Veterans Affairs turned his Department around when he took over that portfolio. He made massive changes based on the premise of giving the veteran the benefit of the doubt.
That is what the motion of the Hon. Member for York Centre does. It gives the benefit of the doubt to those individuals who, through no fault of their own, through no attempt to beat the system, find themselves in an overpayment situation and unable to deal properly with it. I hope the Government is listening.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   SOCIAL SERVICES OVERPAYMENTS TO BENEFICIARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is certainly an important motion introduced into the House by the Hon. Member. It is important because today there are thousands of Canadians who have third party attachments on their wages. The province you are in determines how much money you get out of your cheque. If you are the only person working in a family of four, in most of the provinces you can be assured that all you will get from your cheque is less than $200 a week because of a third party attachment placed there by the Government of Canada for an overpayment you received.
When you look at the Auditor General's report you always see-and this is what makes the news-that under such and such a program millions and millions of dollars were paid out to people who were not eligible to receive those payments. We were talking about unemployment insurance a minute ago. All those payments are called overpayments.
I listened very carefully to what the hon. gentleman who introduced the motion said and then to what the government spokesperson said following his address. What she said sounded very fair. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, that you owe the Government of Canada money as hundreds of thousands of Canadians presently do through no fault of their own. They are receiving a benefit from unemployment insurance or any of our social security programs. Of course, the rules vary from the Department of Verteran Affairs to National Revenue or the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
Thousands of people go before judges. I always recall the words of one of the foremost authorities on overpayments in Canada today. His name is Justice Dubinsky. He is a Federal Appeals Court Judge. He always says that the forgiveness of the overpayment is in the hands of the Minister or, in the case of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, in the hands of the Commission. He knows they cannot afford to pay it back but he cannot do anything about that. The court, in Canada, is not authorized to forgive an overpayment. That is in the hands of the Minister or the Commission.
The Hon. Member who spoke on behalf of the Government sounded very eloquent when she said "in cases of undue hardship", or did she say "in the case of extreme hardship"? I am not sure which she used because the wording differs in various regulations. "Undue hardship" is the most common expression.
In the case of undue hardship the Minister may-not shall-forgive the overpayment, or if it costs more money to collect it than the Government will get back, it does not collect it. She mentioned another one which does not apply to all social legislation, that is, if the error is made by an official of the Department it shall be deemed not to be paid back by the person who received the money.
The fact is that there are thousands of people in Canada today who are getting $120 a week to feed their families because there is a third party attachment on their wages by the Government. These are not rich people. These are people who had overpayments on a social security benefit, not from the stock market.
Members of Parliament go before a judge on behalf of constituents to say that a constituent should not have to repay a that particular overpayment. It was not his fault. He did not do anything wrong.
An Hon. Member mentioned a few moments ago cases he had where the Unemployment Insurance Commission made a mistake. The funny part about it is that it did not make a mistake because an overpayment and the determination of eligibility do not rest with the Department of Employment and Immigration. They rest with National Revenue.
When one applies for benefits, the official fills out the form, sends it in, and the cheque is sent. The error takes places after because the determination of eligibility in the case of the largest social security program in this country, unemployment insurance, is made by National Revenue. It has nothing to do with the Unemployment Insurance Commission. The Unemployment Insurance Commission has no more to do with determining eligibility of a person drawing unemployment insurance than I do with going to the moon.
September 23, 1988

Who has made the mistake? No one has made the mistake. The official down in National Revenue perhaps made a correct judgment. Let me give an example. An accountant working for a company by the name of Beothic in eastern Canada, which deals with fish products, was wrong and therefore made incorrect receipts for people who sold to that company. Therefore, 293 people now have to pay back to the Government amounts varying from $2,000 to $30,000. That occurred within the last two years.
I could list other cases where many people have been trapped by this. Somebody will say that they received a letter from the Government of Canada saying that they owe a certain amount of money. They want to know why. Is it because an accountant made a mistake in a company? The person, according to the law of Canada, under all these programs, is responsible for paying it back if a mistake is made even by the government Department concerned. That is in the Unemployment Insurance Act that the hon. gentleman was quoting a few moments ago.
The problem is that the Minister will not use the ministerial authority granted under the Act to forgive those payments. That is the problem.
There is only one other way to overcome the problem. It is to drag it out long enough in the courts to go beyond the three years which is normally the period after which one cannot be held accountable for money owed to the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Stretch it out as long as you can, ask for an adjournment or a postponement until you get to the point where they cannot collect it anyway. That is the only choice.
However, if people do not work the system that way or cannot afford the lawyers, in some cases they are left with having third party attachments on all their wages and end up getting anywhere from $120 to $190 a week regardless of the size of their family until the money is paid back. That is wrong.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   SOCIAL SERVICES OVERPAYMENTS TO BENEFICIARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission, I too would like to speak to Motion M-167 introduced by the Hon. Member for York Center (Mr. Kaplan). He proposes that the Government consider the advisability of prohibiting any federal department or agency which has in error made an overpayment to an individual under a social program from claiming repayment or withholding the overpayment from future payments to the individual, unless the individual is responsible directly or indirectly for the error.
On April 26, 1988, the Hon. Member also suggested to the House that the Government should not demand repayment for excess amounts when the recipient is not responsible for the error.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure we all share the basic sentiments expressed in the Hon. Member's motion. The federal Government would rather not make life any harder than it is for
Social Services
people drawing such social benefits as those paid under old age security, the Canada Pension Plan, or family allowances. We are aware that the recipients generally have a low income and cannot readily cope with reduced benefits.
1 would point out to Hon. Members that the federal Government thinks it is important for Canadian men and women who are in a difficult financial situation to know that the amount of their benefits will not be reduced overnight. As an example, Mr. Speaker, I would say that under the income security programs which I just mentionned and which are administered by the Department of National Health and Welfare the procedure followed to recoup overpayments is very flexible indeed. In difficult circumstances, overpayments may be repaid in very low instalments, in fact as little as $1 a month in the case of people with limited income.
In additoin, Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the Old Age Security Act, the Familly Allowances Act and the Canada Pension Plan the Minister may waive such repayments in extraordinary circumstances, including unforseen difficulties, erroneous advice or administrative mistakes on the part of the Government.
The federal Government can appreciate the situation of low income and underprivileged Canadians, but still it has to answer to the taxpayers.
Overpayments under social benefit programs are debts against the Crown and if they are not recouped they must be offset through higher tax levies on all Canadians. After all, it boils down to financial responsibility, and I would suggest that this federal Government has done very well in that respect.
In the discharge of our mandate we have maintained a policy to recoup excess benefits by using procedures which respect both the people who are overpaid and the taxpayers of the country, but every year such overpayments still account for millions of dollars in government outlays.
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, no system is perfect. Further, simple solutions to the problem might lead to new problems in other areas. The Hon. Member's motion in my view is a good example. If implemented, his proposal would require a new, complex, and costly bureaucratic process to determine whether the claimant is directly or indirectly responsible for the error that led to the overpayment.
This process could be long and arduous, and generate various delays. Participation from public servants, judges and lawyers could be needed, as well as a relevant appeal mechanism. In addition to imposing a new burden on public servants and taxpayers, such a system no doubt would be frustrating and confusing for claimants, especially where their own testimony could be the only available evidence to determine whether an error had been made or not. No doubt, in a great many cases, a clear and satisfactory decision might be impossible. Therefore, such a system could lead both to a miscarriage of justice where the evidence was limited, unsupported or unverifiable.

September 23, 1988
Social Services
Some people might suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there is another solution than the existing systems or the one put forward by the Hon. Member's motion, namely that the Government should delay initial payments on social programs until an absolutely accurate computation of benefits can be made. Or, alternatively, it could be suggested that the Government should make smaller payments while waiting for further information concerning the computation of benefits.
Such a procedure, Mr. Speaker, could however do significant harm to a number of claimants. For instance, one could wait up to two years after the initial benefit payment in order for the current Canada Pension Plan benefits to be adjusted based on an updating of the claimant's gains by Revenue Canada.
Similarly, benefits based on income under federal programs such as Guaranteed Income Supplement and Spouse Allocation normally are calculated on the claimant's income during the previous year for income tax purposes; under certain circumstances, they can be based on an estimation of the claimant's current income, subject to possible review.
Overpayments made in either of those cases would not necessarily be the claimant's fault. It is my view that serious attention should be paid to the matter before introducing a system, the underlying principle of which would be that an error can always be blamed beyond the shadow of a doubt to someone. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, when considering the practicality of the Hon. Member's motion and any relevant proposal, legislators should evaluate whether those very real negative impacts would be warranted.
As I explained, the ways used by the Canadian Government to recover overpayments made under social programs are both sensitive and flexible to Canadians who receive those overpayments, and they are indicative of this Government's responsible attitude toward Canadian taxpayers.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   SOCIAL SERVICES OVERPAYMENTS TO BENEFICIARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to join in the debate this afternoon on the issue raised by the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan). I am sure we all have sympathy for people who, through no fault of their own, are suddenly asked to make a substantial repayment of an overpayment to them. The bewilderment, the panic, even the anger involved must be considerable.
We have heard already this afternoon that there are a number of safeguards in place to protect Canadians who have been overpaid unwittingly by federal Departments. I would suggest that the worthy objectives in the motion before us have already been met or can be met provided those safeguards are compassionately administered.
In effect, this motion calls for the House to make a blanket amnesty for anyone who was overpaid. In other words: "Keep the extra money. Good luck to you on the windfall". The only people who would be asked to repay money to the Crown under the motion are those who are responsible directly or indirectly for the error. I think of the recent case three or four months ago involving a women, who I think lives here in Ontario, who received a cheque from the Department of National Revenue, 1 believe, for several hundred thousand dollars, thanks to a computer gone wild. On the plain reading of the motion before us today there would be no discretion whatsoever in the Minister or the Crown. They would be obligated to allow this person to keep that type of windfall. 1 think that where the public's money is involved we have to do better than that. I believe we need more checks and balances than that.
I believe that in order to judge whether any new legislation is needed we should first see how the present regulations are working.
I wish to take a few minutes to look at one Department in particular. Reference has already been made to it by the Hon. Member from the New Democratic Party who spoke earlier. I refer to the Department of Veterans Affairs. This is a Department which sends out over 200,000 cheques every month. Disability pensions, which are not subject to a means test, account for 144,000 of those monthly cheques.
With such a volume it is not surprising that overpayments are made from time to time. For instance, a veteran may die and his widow may forget to inform Veterans Affairs of his death for a period of time.
Naturally, every possible effort is made to recover these overpayments. It is worth noting that the recovery rate is in the 90 per cent to 95 per cent range. What that tells us is that Canadians are honest. They do not want to receive a benefit to which they are not entitled. They are very understanding when they realize that they have received money and are not entitled to it. Generally, they are quite willing to pay it back.
For the other 10 per cent or so this is where the safeguards come in. When it is plain that recovery in whole or in part could result in undue hardship to a veteran or his family, a recommendation for recovery of a partial settlement or for a total write-off is made under Section 18 of the Financial Administration Act.
It is important to know that recommendations for write-offs are also considered seriously when it is clearly evident that an overpayment was due to an administrative error.
I want to outline how Veterans Affairs handles the question of overpayments involving war veterans and civilian war allowances. These benefits are only paid to needy veterans. In other words, they are subject to a means test.
September 23, 1988

There are over 64,000 veterans or their families receiving allowances. Given the average age of this clientele overpayments do occur. The whole nature of the allowance program means that at age 65 the male veteran becomes eligible for Health and Welfare support programs and so is less dependent on Veterans Affairs.
Because of this transition the War Veterans Allowance Program administration was overhauled in 1986 in order to cut down on overpayments. It is now closely aligned to the Guaranteed Income Supplement and spouses' allowance programs of Health and Welfare. This alignment I am advised has greatly reduced the chance and the number of overpayments.
One key improvement was the annual reporting by war veterans allowance recipients of changes in their financial status and the subsequent adjustment of Veterans Affairs in the annual rate of payment. But overpayments still do occur, and doubtless always will.
I think it is instructive to see how Veterans Affairs deals with these overpayments. The then Minister of Veterans Affairs, the Hon. Member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees), told his Department in 1984 when we formed the Government that he wanted all veterans and their dependants to be treated with the utmost generosity. That instruction has been followed to the letter when it comes to overpayments. The remission of an overpayment is usually the most favoured position.
I think this is illustrated by the operational guidelines given to to those involved with the allowance program. 1 would like to quote the opening paragraphs in full because I think they render this motion unnecessary. They state:
The very nature of the services provided under the Acts and Regulations administered under the direction of the Minister of Veterans Affairs dictates that the general policy and overriding principle to be considered in the handling of overpayments must be one that is based on justice, equity, compassion and human dignity.
Translated into practice, this means that all cases, remission of an overpayment must be considered before any further action is taken. If it has been determined that the overpayments are not eligible for remission, the subsequent recovery or deletion action should never, in any case, deprive the veterans or his dependants of any moneys required to live in dignity.
1 suggest that those instructions to bureaucrats on the front line are more compassionate and effective than any new legislation we could pass today.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   SOCIAL SERVICES OVERPAYMENTS TO BENEFICIARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak today to motion No. 167 which was moved by the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) and which states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of prohibiting-
Already the wording of the motion seems to indicate that there is something tortuous about this.
As 1 was listening to his remarks a while ago, I could not help wondering how it is that as a former Solicitor General and Cabinet Minister, he could move such a motion.
Social Services
How can he ask the Government to consider the advisability of not seeking repayment when an overpayment has occurred? Does he not realize that such a situation could be interpreted as a way for the Government to encourage incompetence and for the individual to justify keeping the money by arguing: I may not be entitled to this money, but why should I advise them of this overpayment, since they are not going to ask me to pay it back? I suggest that we are here to develop and emphasize the competence of our employees and also promote integrity.
Mr. Speaker, it is clear that such a motion will look very nice in Hansard or in householder mailings. Yet, this Hon. Member who sat on Government benches for 15 years would have been taken much more seriously if he had moved this motion at that time, instead of waiting until he sits in the Opposition. But since we live in a democratic system, I will deal with this proposal. If I may, I should like to develop the two major ideas I put across a while ago by providing concrete examples associated with the unemployment insurance scheme. A great many people have visited my office-you know how in a hurry people are when they visit their elected representatives-to ask me to rush a decision concerning an employment insurance application. It is not dishonest but quite normal. When a man or woman working in the Beauharnois- Salaberry riding-or any city or town for that matter-does not get his or her unemployment insurance benefits they pay us a visit and accuse federal employees of procrastinating, for they have bills to pay.
Our employees, on the other hand, must be very careful with our taxpayers' money, they have to go by the book, and 1 am full of admiration for all those working in unemployment insurance offices who always hear bad news and never good news. As their former Parliamentary Secretary, 1 saw the long line-ups in the morning and I am full of admiration. It is a job that has to be done, but let me tell you that you forget about the 3, 200 others who got their cheques in time when every morning you get complaints from 40 or 50 people who blame the delays on your incompetence.
What's happening, for example, at the Unemployment Insurance Commission? What would happen in a Commission or Government where the staff are not responsible or where they are . . . But how far can responsibility take us? If a civil servant makes an error resulting in an overpayment, can the Government claim repayment? I think that government officials would be the first to be unhappy with such a law because it would minimize their role and bring discredit upon the civil service. People could ask John Doe: "Why don't you make a mistake and give me just a little more; it doesn't matter since they can't touch you." I am sure that most if not all our civil servants are honest people and would not entertain such a suggestion. That is primarily why they try to respect the laws and regulations. On the other hand, as I said a few moments ago, I don't know if most citizens would be happy with such a law that, in fact, encourages a certain flexibility in its enforcement.

September 23, 1988
Social Services
If I were to get $2,000 more than I usually draw in family allowances it seems to me I would notice. The fact that I get an extra $2,000 in benefits does not automatically mean that it is due to me, it is something that does not belong to me!
What is to be done for example in a case like the unemployment insurance incident 1 referred to earlier? People imagine that if the UIC paid $2,000 too much it was not aware of it. Imagine a citizen saying he did not know! "If you got an overpayment of $2,000 you have to pay it back!" Generally speaking, I must say that people were aware of it.
Again recently, unemployment insurance recipients came to see me at my office. Yet we know very well that full-time students are not entitled to unemployment benefits. He was overpaid by mistake because the inquiry had not been completed and a false statement was made.
In such cases, Mr. Speaker, the Unemployment Insurance Commission takes the situation into account. In the case I just mentioned there are two important elements: first an administrative error and, second, a false statement. This is altogether different from a case where there has been a clerical error, for example, and the individual receives a cheque for $182 when in fact the benefits should not be more than $172. I can understand an average man not realizing he is getting $10 more a week. But I am sure he can tell the difference when he aplies for unemployment benefits to which he is not entitled.
Mr. Speaker, the UIC takes into account specific cases and the situation of the person who has been overpaid. Where for instance repaying the overpayment leads to undue hardship, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, and I am convinced that the appropriate afficials should, where there has been no dishonesty, schedule repayments so that the claimant can refund within the prescribed period, while abiding by the existing Act and regulations.
Mr. Speaker, this is a very simple concept because it takes responsibility into account. We, as managers of the Unemployment Insurance Fund, are using our money, not only government money. One third of the money comes from the Government. As we know there are three partners in this. . .
employers and taxpayers also are involved. We have absolutely no right to be free-handed in the management of assets that come from the Government. But we have no right either, and still much less, to be free handed with moneys that are entrusted to us by taxpayers, moneys entrusted to us by companies and moneys contributed by the employees.
Because of the very nature of payments and the source of those funds, we must make absolutely sure that we are dealing fairly with all Canadians. It would be unfair, for instance, to those who had contributed, if an overpayment caused by an administrative error, is automatically written off. Some might suggest that the matter already was dealt with in another Private Member's Bill, right at the beginning, I remember it was in 1984 or 1985; it said that any debt to Revenue Canada should be written off. Well, simply preparing my income tax return and stating that I owe a debt and I will have it written-off.. . Nothing is as simple nor as nice!
Administrative errors of this kind reflect badly on our competence.
In closing, I repeat that federal employees must be guided by legislation which bars them from making negative value judgments. They also need such legislation for their own personal satisfaction. An honest citizens also want the money they provide for the poor to be spent wisely because, all too often, people jump to conclusions.
